newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: S.Africa ostrich farmers see EU ban lifted soon.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa ostrich farmers see EU ban lifted soon.

text.p: South African ostrich farmers attending an industry conference in the Netherlands on Friday said they hoped the European Union would lift its ban on ostrich meat and live birds within a month.
The EU imposed the ban on Thursday following an outbreak of Congo fever at one of South Africa's main ostrich abattoirs, threatening a multi-million rand export business.

Speaking at the European Ostrich Association's 1996 World Congress they insisted South African ostrich meat was safe to eat and the industry had measures in place to prevent the spread of the fever, which has killed one abattoir worker.
"The ban will be uncomfortable for the industry but I'm sure it will be lifted soon. I would think 30 days would be enough," Scoop Pienaar of the African Game and Export Co said.

"The department of public health immediately isolated the abattoir after the incident. The standard of hygiene imposed by the European Union is very strict," Pienaar said, adding that around one million rand's ($213,900) worth of meat had been destroyed.
The two-day conference, attracting some 300 participants from around 25 countries was aimed at promoting ostrich rearing.

In Europe the industry has grown rapidly in recent years, benefiting from the recent "mad cow disease" health scare. Ostrich, a dark meat similar to beef, now features on many restaurant menus and has even been used in British Airways' in-flight meals.
"It's great for people looking for an easy meat to cook, and it has less fat and cholesterol than beef," said Fred van der Horst, vice-chairman of the European Ostrich Association (EOA).
"A few years ago the Netherlands imported 100 tonnes of meat a year, now it's 400 tonnes and growing."

The scare over British beef may have prompted the European Commission to act quickly in this case but veterinary experts at the conference said there was no danger of the tick-borne Congo fever spreading to the Europe's ostrich stock.
"This is a tick-borne fever and the (Congo) tick cannot survive in Europe," said Dr Gerry Dorrestein of Utrecht University's Veterinary Medicine faculty and advisor to the EOA.
"It is here in Europe that the cycle (in the disease spreading to humans) would be broken."

Congo-Crimean haemorrhagic fever is an infectious disease which, like the notorious viral disease Ebola, causes body organs to degenerate with massive internal and some external bleeding. About 30 percent of Congo fever cases are fatal.
Exports from South African ostriches are worth millions of rands a year, and represent some 85 percent of the world market.

Ostrich leather exports exceed 400 milllion rand ($85 million) each year while an average of 16 million tonnes of meat valued at 58 million rand is exported annually, according to the South African agriculture department.
A tick bite caused South Africa's first case of Congo fever in 1981 and sporadic cases have occurred since in rural areas. ($1=4.6735 Rand)
